subsubtopic: INFORMATION NEEDED FOR FILING CLAIMS-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the deadline for the filing of income tax forms is only weeks away, yet this year taxpayers and officials in the Department of National Revenue are caught in a horrible muddle. Officials are advising taxpayers to complete their forms as if proposed tax measures contained in the budget of last November were law, or face retroactive charges with interest penalties. Taxpayers following these instructions are also being told that no tax returns Tilled out according to the budget will be processed by the department until the measures in the budget become law. People claiming refunds could be waiting for their money for a long time. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That the Minister of Finance immediately present his tax change measures to the House for debate; Canadian taxpayers must be able to file claims based on actual, not hypothetical legislation, and officials in the Department of National Revenue must have the authority to process these claims.

Since the 1950s the Micmac Indians of Newfoundland, instead of being registered as Indians under the Indian Act, have been administered by the province through a federal-provincial agreement, which therefore denies these Indians the right to entitlements under the Indian Act. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly):

The NDP government of Saskatchewan last week legislated striking hospital workers in the province back to their jobs, even though they were on a legal strike. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In western Canada the spectre of separation is a growing movement. One separatist was elected in Alberta, hundreds are turning out to meetings, and it appears the Western Canada Concept will run any number of candidates in the coming Saskatchewan provincial election. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen):
That this House, rather than condemn the separatists, to form a special parliamentary task force to study the anger and frustration of western Canadians in order that remedial action may be taken by the government to end the threat of secession and keep this country together.

subtopic: THE HONOURABLE MEMBER FOR WINNIPEG NORTH CENTRE
speechtext: I believe the House has said it all. I do want to wish the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) our warmest welcome and to tell him how much we all love him.

subtopic: THE HONOURABLE MEMBER FOR WINNIPEG NORTH CENTRE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: THE HONOURABLE MEMBER FOR WINNIPEG NORTH CENTRE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker and friends, 1 thank you indeed for your kindness and for welcoming me back here after these long six months. I am very grateful for this opportunity to say a few words of appreciation.
First, 1 want to say thanks to members of my family, to my friends from this House of Commons, and to others who have done so much for me during the past six months. Also, I want to say a word about the people in the hospitals where I spent considerable time. They are the most wonderful people. 1 refer to those at the hospital on Carling Avenue and to those at the hospital on Smyth Road. They have been just tremendous. The doctors, the nurses and the workers have been wonderful and they made me feel that there was a chance, despite my serious illness, that I might come back.

subtopic: THE HONOURABLE MEMBER FOR WINNIPEG NORTH CENTRE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: THE HONOURABLE MEMBER FOR WINNIPEG NORTH CENTRE
speechtext:
I have here a piece of paper so 1 would be sure to get the right names. One of my problems, of course, with this illness is that I have a little trouble with my memory, but at any rate I am doing fine.
At the same time, Madam Speaker, having expressed my appreciation of so many people and so much help, and for the fact that what had seemed hopeless now seems to be coming along-at least I can get back here-there are two people in particular whom I would like to mention because of the special help they gave me. Those two people are Norman Smith of Ottawa and Jim Sinclair of Vancouver. About six years ago both of these friends of mine had an illness almost as serious as mine; not to the full extent, but it was the end of everything for
Mr. Knowles
them. Yet somehow the hospitals, doctors and other people helped them to try to make things better.
What did these two men do? One wrote me a letter from Vancouver, and the other came to see me in Ottawa. They did this because they wanted to encourage me to do my best to make it back. I have to say to my friends who know about it that that experience has meant a great deal to me, and I thank in particular Norman Smith and Jim Sinclair.
I thank everyone for the reception you have given me here today. I cannot be here every day because I have to go back to the hospital two days a week for therapy and so on, but 1 will get fully back as soon as 1 can. It means a great deal to me to have the kind of reception you have given me today. Thank you very much.
[Whereupon the House rose a second time and applauded.]

Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, I will direct my question to the right hon. Prime Minister. On August 4, 1977, in this House, the Minister of Finance, who was then the President of the Privy Council, told us that the Alaska natural gas pipeline would create, during its construction phase, 25,000 direct man-years of employment and 220,000 indirect man-years, mainly in the manufacturing sector in central Canada. These jobs were further confirmed by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources when he assured us that he had an ironclad guarantee that this pipeline would proceed.
In view of the continuing delay in the construction of the pipeline, I wonder if the Prime Minister can give this House and the jobless of Canada any ironclad guarantee that they will ultimately be the beneficiaries of the government's promises.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in so far as this government is concerned, I can give that guarantee. We have the evidence given by the government when it moved and permitted the pre-build, which was an indication of this government's commitment to that pipeline. In so far as being able to guarantee the performance of another government, we will do our best to ensure that the spirit with which that agreement was entered into by President Carter and myself will be respected by the present administration.

Through Your Honour, may 1 draw the Prime Minister's attention to the fact that every major energy project that his Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has touched has been a disaster? Alsands and Cold Lake, the magaprojects, have been either delayed or cancelled. Two hundred and twenty-six conventional oil and gas drilling rigs have fled the country, and now the gas pipeline has been delayed yet another time. Can the Prime Minister name any significant energy-related project that will proceed? When will such project commence construction? As a result, how many jobless will be taken off the welfare and unemployment rolls and put to work where they belong and where they want to be?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the question seems somewhat rhetorical in character.
I would point out to the hon. member that many energy-related projects have begun and are proceeding. The Q & M PipeLines is one example. The hon. member mentioned the tar sands. I think it is premature to say that that megaproject will not proceed. There was an agreement announced yesterday, I
believe, between the Government of Alberta and the Government of Canada indicating that they were still seeking a solution. However, 1 would point out to the hon. member that as he knows, in this House, for the past 18 months, the federal Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has been indicating government support and agreement to the terms requested by Alsands. He will recall that it was the Premier of Alberta who held up that project for the simple reason he gave, that he did not want the Alsands to proceed until the energy agreement was signed. I think, viewed with hindsight, that was a regrettable position taken by the Premier of Alberta.
Pass the buck.

subsubtopic: INVOLVEMENT IN GENERAL MOTORS CORPORATION DEAL WITH IRAQ
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for International Trade. As the minister knows, the automotive quota agreement with Japan expires today with no renewal arrangements in sight. To add insult to injury, the GM-Iraq deal for 12,500 Malibus has fallen through, even after the minister has bragged about that deal for over a year. Now we hear that there was no formal contract, yet 80 million tax dollars are at stake with the Export Development Corporation. Normal procedure or not, I, for one, along with my party and, more important, the taxpayer, find this to be totally unacceptable. Therefore I would like to ask the minister to tell this House how he and his bumbling colleagues in cabinet could endorse the Export Development Corporation's involvement in a deal where there was no formal agreement on this last 12,500 cars-even after the minister's numerous trips to Baghdad.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of State (International Trade)):
subsubtopic: INVOLVEMENT IN GENERAL MOTORS CORPORATION DEAL WITH IRAQ
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member has asked a multitude of questions in that one. First of all, it is normal international practice that the export supply agencies insure payment obligations by foreign customers to Canadian exporters, or exporters to a particular country.
In this particular case we have had no evidence that there is a bona fide contract, so at this point in time the Government of Canada and the people of Canada are not obligated for one single cent.

speechtext:
Although the EDC agrees that it is normal practice, it will be reponsible for $80 million of the taxpayers' money in this regard. I am wondering whether the minister is saying that he expects the taxpayer to foot the bill for $80 million for these blunders. Is that what he is saying?
March 31, 1982

Surely he is irresponsible as an administrator for the government when he allows this deal to go through, patting himself on the back all the year round, without a formal ironclad contract being established. Therefore 1 want him to tell this House, first of all, was he aware that General Motors already filed a claim with the EDC on February 27 and secondly, what is he going to do to save the taxpayers from footing the bill for this $80 million for this funded program that he put together and that the minister has bragged about all the year. I suggest that he has no answers and, if he does not have the answers, could he bring the whole matter to the appropriate committee for proper consideration?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of State (International Trade)):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REFERRAL TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as I said earlier, at this point in time the people of Canada are not obligated for one single cent of this particular transaction. No bona fide contract has been put forward to the Export Development Corporation. Since 1944 the Export Development Corporation, and its predecessor, have insured contracts all around the world on behalf of Canadian exporters. Only once in one year during that whole period have they lost any money. As a matter of fact, 99.6 per cent of all contracts insured are paid for by the customers. The scare tactics used by the opposition, and by the hon. member, as usual are invalid.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have one final supplementary. The minister did not respond to my question as to whether he is aware that General Motors in fact did put a claim in to the EDC on February 27. That is one question to which 1 wanted an answer. Second, if he is so sure of himself, can he guarantee to this House and the Canadian taxpayer that in fact the Canadian taxpayer through the EDC is not going to be responsible for one red cent for the blundering program that the minister introduced as far as this agreement or arrangement is concerned?

No announcement has ever come forward from General Motors or from the Government of Canada, or from the Export Development Corporation, regarding the sale of the next 12,000 cars. 1 am aware that General Motors has put forth a claim but, as I said here on three previous occasions, I am advised that they have not forwarded any bona fide contracts and consequently, as far as the Government of Canada and the Export Development Corporation are concerned, at the present time there is no obligation on behalf of the people of Canada.
Oral Questions ENERGY

Madam Speaker, I regret the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is not in the House today. Perhaps 1 could direct my question to the Prime Minister. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has repeatedly told this House that there is a limit to how much of the taxpayers' money is to be thrown into the Alsands project. Yesterday the government threw another $8 million into this project, a gift to the corporate oil fraternity, to keep them interested in the project for another month. Oil representatives are saying that because of the drop in world oil prices there is little chance that the oil project can be saved, in spite of the $8 million. 1 would like to ask the Prime Minister when is the government going to admit what appears obvious to everybody else, that unless tremendous and massive tax concessions are granted to the companies participating in the Alsands project, it is not going to go ahead.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it seems to me that that is the very subject which is, to the knowledge of the House, being discussed between the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the persons involved in the Alsands project and the Government of Alberta.
The hon. member mentions the two governments putting money in to keep the project open for discussion one more month. He, of course, realizes that the two governments have a large equity position in Alsands. It is normal for them to want this matter to be resolved in the interests not only of the people of Alberta but of the people of Canada who, as the hon. member points out, include the consumers of energy. This also involves a very high number of jobs which would go with the proceeding of this project. That is the subject matter of the negotiations that are going on which have a deadline of less than a month from now, and which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will report on when he is in the House.

Madam Speaker, I am certain that the public is particularly interested in the question of how much public funding, regardless of equity, the government is prepared to throw into this project, because Alsands looks risky both in terms of job creation and the per barrel price of oil. Has the government considered taking action on some alternative processes for the same money, such as enhanced recovery, which can produce oil at a lot cheaper per barrel price, and going further into the heavy oil instead of synthetic at Alsands?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on the price of oil, I think the hon. member would have a good point if he were certain that the price of world oil would forever and a day remain low and not return to the kind of escalation we have known since 1973. That is the basic

March 31, 1982
Oral Questions
question on which everyone connected with the business will have to make up his mind. Do we want to become self-reliant in Canada with oil which might be higher priced than world oil, or will world oil go up higher than tar sands oil? Will we then be happy to have had even this high-priced oil produced in Canada? I repeat, the question is being debated now.
1 find it a bit singular that the hon. member would suggest alternate uses for these funds. I remember I was making that argument about a year and a half ago before progress had been made with the Alsands, and pointing out that there were alternate sources, those that the hon. member mentions, the offshore oil around Hibernia, and the Beaufort Sea oil. There are many areas where we can go.
1 point out to the hon. member that then it was his party, and more specifically the leader of his party, who was saying that if the private sector was not going ahead with Alsands, the people of Canada through the government should be financing and putting money into it. How can he reverse his position so easily with this kind of hindsight? He should consult with his leader who was telling us to put more money into Alsands. He is now telling us to put less.

As far as reversing positions is concerned, for the past 14 years I have been staring across at the Prime Minister. We have learned something about that. 1 do not agree that we have reversed our position at all.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege, of which I have given you notice and which you indicated to me that you were
prepared to hear under Standing Order 17(2). It concerns misleading statements made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) as reported in Hansard on March 22, 1982, on which day she was allowed to answer three questions. These questions appear in Hansard at pages 15666, 15667 and 15671 and they dealt with the status of Indian women. In her replies to those questions, the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated that no Indian woman had lost her status during her time in cabinet. Subsequent to that, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) indicated through the press that the statement of the Minister of National Health and Welfare was incorrect. Indeed, 1,810 Indian women have lost their status between 1976 and 1980. In a press release, the minister commented that what Madam Begin did was to equate enfranchisement-the right to vote-with status. I understand the minister was confused between enfranchisement-the right to vote-and the loss of status. That does indicate her confusion and the extent of it, because the loss of status is a much more serious question than the loss of the right to vote, serious as that right is. The loss of status means the loss of culture, the loss of identity and the loss of being as an Indian person. She indicated to the House that no such loss had occurred to any Indian woman during the time she had been a cabinet minister. I ask, Madam Speaker, that the minister rise in her place-and I quite understand her confusion-and correct her statements for the record in Hansard. She could have done that previously, but I would like her to do it now.
My question of privilege is that there has been a misleading statement made here in the House which we would like to see corrected. As long as it remains on the record of the House of Commons, it is indeed a question of privilege which concerns all Members of Parliament who have been misled by a minister of the Crown.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I support what the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) has said. If you look at the remarks of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) as reported on page 15667 of Hansard, you will find seven instances of remarks which reflect upon the member asking the question, such as:
The hon. member has made innuendoes that are not acceptable, beginning with a false quotation which I would like him to check and correct . .. the hon. member should state the complete situation .. . the hon. member's questions are among the most dangerous ones I have ever heard in the House-
We have waited, Madam Speaker, for the minister to come forward with the truth and set the record straight. If you do not allow this question to be put to the minister, then the record will stand as condemning members on this side with those words. The reason we ask that you allow this question to be put is to set the record straight. Hansard is the history of this House, and we do not want these remarks to remain on the record in their present form.
March 31, 1982

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have had an opportunity to examine the statements made with regard to this matter, and I think it is unfortunate that the question went as far as it did. In looking at your comments I see that you were trying to be generous because you were not at first clear as to whether or not the question did in fact fall under the jurisdiction of the minister. Beauchesne's states in Citation 359(10):
A question ought not to refer to a statement made outside the House by a minister.
That is the first point on which we seem to have got off the track. Citation 359 also says in part:
A brief question seeking information about an important matter of some urgency which falls within the administrative responsibility of the government or of the specific minister to whom it is addressed-
And then Citation 359(6) says:
The minister to whom the question is directed is responsible to the House for his present ministry-
On page 329 of the nineteenth edition of Erskine May it
says:
Questions to ministers must relate to matters for which those ministers are officially responsible.
I suggest, Madam Speaker, that that ends the matter. I think you have disposed of this matter according to Beauchesne's, Erskine May and according to precedent. I see no other solution, unless we are to break with all tradition and precedent of parliamentary procedure.

Madam Speaker, you will recall that what gave rise to this question was a speech by the minister made in Vancouver where she said it was her responsibility and that of other female members of cabinet to approve certain orders in council which affect the status and rights of native women. It was on the basis of her responsibility that this question was asked, because in her speech she said no Indian person had lost her status in the time that she, the minister, had been discharging this responsibility in cabinet.
The minister explained to the audience in her speech, quoted in the House, what her direct responsibilities were. Obviously she was confused, and she should have the opportunity to clear up this matter on her own behalf and on behalf of native people.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think I made it quite clear in my intervention the other day that I was in doubt about whether or not the question should be allowed, but I let it go because things do happen very quickly in question period. I now know for sure that the question should not have been allowed to be directed to that particular minister. It might have been allowed to another minister, but not to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) because it was not within the realm of her administrative responsibilities. I let it go and the procedure did suffer a bit because it ought not to have been allowed. I do regret that and ask the indulgence of the House.
There was a question posed, not repeated today, that since I had allowed those questions then, should I not allow the
Privilege-Miss MacDonald
questions that were asked yesterday. The fact that there was a slip in procedure on one day of course does not mean that the rules of the House should be altered. Therefore, since I was very sure that the questions yesterday did not relate to the administrative responsibilities of the minister, I did now allow them. I repeat, the questions might have been directed to another minister whose responsibility it is to answer them.
As to the question of privilege put forward by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), the fact that the statement might be judged to be misleading by a member of the House, of course, does not constitute the basis for a question of privilege. That is a matter of judgment. The hon. member might feel it is misleading, as is her right, but it is a matter of judgment and does not constitute the basis for a question of privilege. The only circumstances under which that might be considered to be the basis of a question of privilege is if the statement had been deliberately misleading, and that charge would have to be made.
The minister might want to make a statement-
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
-somewhere, either in this House or somewhere else, to clarify the statement, if she feels she should do so. However, that is her choice, and I have no authority to force the minister to make that statement.
Therefore, on those grounds, I cannot find a prima facie case of privilege in the question raised by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, you have just ruled, and the House naturally accepts your ruling. However, we have had a rather difficult situation created here. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), in responding to questions-indeed, as you read Hansard you will see that she asked that questions be directed to her. On page 15671 of Hansard, where I was directing a question to the appropriate minister, the Minister of National Health and Welfare is reported as saying:
Ask me.
In other words, she invited the House of Commons to direct those questions to her. That is very clearly on the record. Indeed, some of us are particularly concerned about the aspersions cast by the minister, in her response, upon hon. members on this side of the House. Her response was an illegitimate response under a strict rendering and reading of the rules. It is, nonetheless, on the record. It is, nonetheless, an aspersion cast upon hon. members on this side of the House which the facts do not merit.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has it within her power, if she acts gracefully, to rectify the situation. When we were putting questions, she said to me, "Ask me the question". As one hon. member of this House to another, I

March 31, 1982
Privilege - Miss MacDonald
would now like to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare to accept her responsibilities, to follow the courtesies of this House and to extend an apology to those hon. members whose names, perhaps inadvertently, she called into question.
There is your chance, Monique.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) knows that this kind of language is constantly used in the House. It is not the first time, and it does not really constitute the basis of a question of privilege. This kind of language is used in debate, and as long as it does not go beyond what is considered to be parliamentary language, I cannot force the minister to withdraw any of those words. If the hon. minister feels that she should withdraw the words she may do so, but it is up to her. However, at this particular point I do not feel I can oblige the Leader of the Opposition. As a matter of fact, he did not ask me to do it. He was only addressing himself to the minister. However, I just want to correctly state for the record that there is no strict obligation for the minister to withdraw her remarks.

Perhaps this is a hypothetical question and, consequently, not one which can be dealt with. However, if the language used by the Minister of National Health and Welfare had been language which the House would normally hold to be unparliamentary, would the fact that she was answering in an illegitimate capacity preclude us from setting the record straight?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would not think so, frankly. Unparliamentary language, as it is spoken, should be a matter for redress. Today, if the hon. minister has chosen to answer, for instance, some of the hon. members who intervened on a question of privilege, I could have allowed the hon. minister to reply. Now the problem has shifted to one of a question of privilege, and any hon. member of this House involved in a question of privilege is free to reply or not to reply.
Madam Speaker, there is another dimension to this problem.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is this a legitimate point of order or is the hon. member just continuing the debate on this particular question? 1 want the hon. member to really consider that before he rises again.

It may be a new question of privilege. Madam Speaker, I really think there is a new dimension to this matter or another dimension which Your Honour has not considered.
Your Honour will recall that, following the exchange between the minister and my colleague, the hon. member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway), I did address the same question to the appropriate minister. It is quite clear to everyone in the House that there is a requirement for an order in
council before the status of an Indian person is denied or cancelled. I asked the minister responsible for native affairs in this country who it was that had signed the order in council to disenfranchise, to remove the status of 1,810 Indian women from 1976 to 1981. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) said she did not sign the order although she had been responsible all those years. That question has not been answered, and we have a right to know the answer.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is debate. That does not enter into the realm of a question of privilege. The hon. member might ask questions in subsequent days at the time of the question period concerning these matters on which he wants to elicit information. However, this is not a question of privilege.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the following questions will be answered today: Nos. 3,448, 3,622, 3,688, 4,051 and 4,124.

Did the Department of the Secretary of State finance in whole or in part the publication of the November, 1981 "Canadian Studies Bulletin" and, if so (a) how many copies were printed and to whom were they distributed (b) what is the objective of the financing of this and similar publications?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext:
The November 1981 issue of the "Canadian Studies Bulletin" was financed by the Canadian Studies Office of the Association of Canadian Community Colleges. The office has received grants from the Secretary of State Department under the National Program of Support for Canadian Studies.
(a)	Three thousand copies were printed and distributed, largely to faculty members in the colleges, institutes and CEGEP's of Canada. Each issue is also mailed to selected individuals in provincial ministries of education, universities, and to members of the federal Parliament. The publication is designed to address issues and areas of interest to educators in post-secondary non-degree-granting institutions.
(b)	The department's objective in financing this kind of publication under its Canadian Studies Program is to disseminate and promote existing resources and information about Canadian materials, and to provide a pan-Canadian platform for the discussion of national issues which concern Canadian educators. More broadly, the program is designed to increase and disseminate knowleldge about Canada by supporting the efforts of organizations and individuals working with all levels of formal and continuing education.

1.	Is there now or was there recently a Statistics Canada survey relating to home security in Halifax, Nova Scotia and, if so (a) what is or was its purpose (b) what questions are or were being asked?
2.	Are or were questions involving salary and personal habits necessary for the survey and, if so, for what reason?
3.	Who has or will have access to the information provided by the respondents?
4.	How many persons in Halifax are being or will be asked the questions and how many persons responded to the questions?

Statistics Canada reports:
1.	(a) Statistics Canada conducted a survey related to the effect of crime on the population (victimization) during the period January 14 to February 26, 1982. The survey included in its coverage Halifax and Dartmouth, Nova Scotia. It contained some questions concerning home security or crime prevention. The survey was conducted for the federal Department of the Solicitor General and its purpose was to obtain information on the frequency and distribution of certain crimes, their impact on victims' perceptions of their experience, their needs and concerns.
(b) The survey included questions about respondent characteristics (age, sex, marital status, income range, etc.) and questions on the respondents' perceptions of the prevalence of crime in their city and neighbourhood, on their attitudes toward the police, and on their use of crime prevention measures. If the respondent had been the victim of certain crimes during 1981, details were collected about each crime, including information on injuries, loss and damage.
2.	The questions concerning personal habits, income and demographic information were necessary and important in identifying the risk of being the victim of a crime for various groups in the population. Previous research has shown that information on personal habits is closely related to the risk of crime.
3.	Statistical information will be made available, in a form that guarantees the confidentiality of respondents, to the Department of the Solicitor General of Canada, to local police departments, and to any person or organization interested in the data.
4.	In the Halifax-Dartmouth area approximately 10,000 households were contacted and although final information is not yet available the response rate is expected to be between 85 and 90 per cent.
5.	(a) The survey was conducted in the greater Vancouver region, the cities of Edmonton and Winnipeg, metropolitan Toronto and Montreal, Halifax-Dartmouth and the city of St. John's.
(b) The number varies by city but in total approximately 70,000 households were contacted. Some 58,490 interviews were completed of which 8,800 approximately were from Halifax-Dartmouth.
6.	The information is being collected under the authority of the Statistics Act which obliges Statistics Canada to safeguard the confidentiality of information provided by respondents. Survey data will be handled only by employees sworn to secrecy under the Statistics Act, and the data will be processed in such a manner that absolutely no information will be released which would allow individuals to be identified.

The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-89, an act to amend the National Housing Act and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works-the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove).

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have examined the motions in amendment to Bill C-89 and I would like to inform the House that Motions Nos. 1 and 2, standing in the name of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney), should be grouped for debate but voted on separately.

Motion No. 1
That Bill C-89, an act to amend the National Housing Act and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, be amended in Clause 1 by striking out line 20 at page I and substituting the following therefor:
"sisting of one or more houses or homes, one or".
Motion No. 2
That Bill C-89, an act to amend the National Housing Act and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, be amended in Clause 25 by striking out line 29 at page 17 and substituting the following therefor:
"sition of his home, including floating homes, for a term that has".
She said: Madam Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to draw to the attention of members of this House a housing need they have probably overlooked when dealing with Bill C-89, that is, the need for floating homes. Most members of the House are spared the ecstacies of west coast living, flowering Japanese plum blossoms and daffodils already in full bloom.
And crocuses?

There is also the ability to use the coastline and the sea as your marine lot.
In moving this amendment, Mr. Speaker, I would like to identify the objective of Motion No. 1 which is to make financing more easily available to residents of floating homes.
The objective of Motion No. 2 is to ensure that the residents of floating homes are eligible for assistance from the federal government in times of soaring interest rates, under the same conditions that all other home owners are eligible for assistance under Bill C-89. This would make this program more equitable.
I would like to point out that floating homes are indigenous to the east coast and the west coast and they are part of our Canadian lifestyle.
Floating homes are becoming increasingly popular as land prices rise and the supply of land dwindles. There are close to 1,000 houseboats and live-aboard boats in the lower mainland area, many of them in my riding of Vancouver Centre.
The major obstacle to the development of floating home communities is the expense of financing. Conventional mortgages are not available. Most people must take out shorter term chattel mortgages or consumer loans at interest rates as high as 21 per cent. This causes great hardship to many people.
1 would like to refer to a letter written to me by one of my constituents who lives on a live-aboard boat, who wrote: "From the mouth of high-ranking Liberals I have heard that no Canadians would be forced to leave their homes because of exorbitant interest rates. 1 am about to lose my home for precisely that reason." This person goes on to detail the increase in mortgage rates from 11.5 per cent to 21 per cent and how even though she and her husband are in the high income group-they are both teachers-they feel they cannot continue. She concludes by saying: "I am appealing to you to bring our case to the attention of anyone whom you can think
March 31, 1982

of who could offer some relief and keep us from losing not only our home but the dream of a lifetime."
Private lending institutions have told me that one of the major reasons they do not arrange mortgages for floating homes is that no mortgage insurance is available for them. Therefore, I seek to amend Bill C-89 through Motion No. 1, to enable Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to provide mortgage insurance for floating home developments.
The purpose of Motion No. 2 is to extend the coverage of the interest deferment plan to include floating homes. Since this government has said that it does not wish to see Canadians lose their homes because of high interest rates, I believe that the owners of floating homes should be eligible for this new program along with other Canadian home owners.
Some members of the House may believe that these amendments are so limited in their application that they are not worthy of consideration, but 1 would argue that it is the purpose of our institutions, including the House of Commons and our banks, to be sensitive to our needs and to accommodate them wherever possible. In particular, Mr. Speaker, a country such as Canada that is bordered by three oceans needs to be aware of the issues which arise on its coasts. Also, a country such as Canada with a growing shortage of affordable housing should also be prepared to consider ideas that would help to meet housing demand.
I would like to list some of the reasons, Mr. Speaker, why floating homes should be encouraged. One is the availability of serviced land for housing development, which is very limited in the lower mainland. According to the greater Vancouver regional district planners, Vancouver is land short, as members from Vancouver are well aware.
Second, land prices are very high and house prices have skyrocketed. In fact, housing prices in Vancouver are the highest in the country, with the average single family dwelling selling for $127,000 and the average condominium for about $92,000 in February, 1982, according to the Vancouver Real Estate Board.
A third reason why floating houses should be encouraged is that water is plentiful. The fourth reason is that house boats are cheaper to build than conventional houses, because, for instance, a two-bedroom 900 square foot house boat, including its water lease, could retail for as low as $85,000-which is at the bottom of the market for Vancouver housing.
Floating homes are good for starter homes or for older couples whose children have left. They would, therefore, help to satisfy part of the housing market.
To be realistic, Mr. Speaker, floating homes will never provide any great deal of housing but they are prime sources of satisfaction to people who choose to make their homes on the water. There have always been people who want to live on the water, ever since Vancouver began as Coal Harbour. In fact, in Vancouver in the early days there used to be quite a floating community, complete with a floating brothel and a whiskey factory. It is traditional for cities on the water, such as London
Housing
and Amsterdam, to have people living on the water. Therefore, this should not be looked on as something strange and new.
In dealing with Vancouver, I would like to make some major points. The first is that this concept of floating homes is technically possible in Vancouver. We have developed sewage systems for house boats. Also, it is physically possible in Vancouver. It is estimated that between 10,000 and 15,000 units could be accommodated in the Vancouver-Victoria area. It is also administratively possible, for the greater Vancouver Regional District has devised construction standards and a model municipal bylaw. It is environmentally possible; there are health codes and fire codes to which house boat communities must conform.
However, the status of floating homes is very vague. Governments do not seem to know what to do with floating homes. For instance, the federal government seems to be in conflict. Revenue Canada treats floating homes like a house. In 1977 the federal government ruled that registered home ownership savings plans could be applied to floating homes; but Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation will not insure mortgages for them or allow floating home residents to be eligible for mortgage assistance under the interest deferment plan. As the minister responsible is in the House, I would like him to note this point.
The provincial government will give the home owners a grant for floating homes that have a land lease. The provincial government also assesses them under the mobile home tax act, but Victoria will not allow them to be included under the mobile home registry act, which means that mortgages on floating homes cannot be registered. This is an important obstacle.
The city of Vancouver classifies marinas as "floating mobile homes covered with water" for the purposes of licences, a wording which is baffling in the extreme. Floating home communities are subject to inspection by a wide range of government officials. These include the fire department, the health department, tax assessors, marine surveyors and the coast guard. They are regulated by municipal bylaw, must comply with the provisions of the regional plan and also come under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, to name some examples.
Most of the obstacles faced by the floating home owners are institutional. First, governments must decide how to deal with floating homes. At present they are forced to conform to a wide range of strict standards, but they receive no consistent treatment under the law. Second, financing must be made more accessible.
I would like first to deal with some of the problems raised by the banks. The banks identify several difficulties with making conventional mortgages available. First, there is nowhere to register the mortgages. Second, since water and land leases are usually for a short term, the rate of depreciation makes amortization over more than ten years impractical. Further, the banks do not know enough about floating homes; they need

March 31, 1982
Housing
more information. Finally, the banks say that another problem is that Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation will not insure these homes under current legislation because of the definition of house, which 1 will speak to later.
None of these obstacles is insurmountable. Floating home mortgages could be registered under the mobile home registry act of British Columbia. If land leases were made available for longer periods, such as 20 years, amortization periods could be extended. More information could be supplied to the banks, and Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation could be empowered to make mortgage insurance available, meeting the requirement of the banks.
Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation also cites several problems for floating home owners. 1 mentioned the first, that there is nowhere to register floating homes. Another point that bothers CMHC is that there is no security. Floating homes can be floated away. Further, the National Housing Act restricts the structures for which insurance is available through its definition of house which is, under current legislation, "a building plus land".
I have already pointed out that the first issue of registration can be resolved. The question of security is more difficult. Owners of floating homes point out that the value of their home declines drastically if it is removed from its mooring. It derives its value and its comfort from its location in a marina. However, CMHC does not accept the argument. It might be possible, however, to meet the corporation's requirements by passing regulations that home owners must secure their house boats to piles and remove the engines in the same way that mobile homes are secured in one place. The point is that if institutions were flexible these problems could be worked out. Finally, my first amendment addresses the issue of mortgage insurance by CMHC.
Since Bill C-89 does not deal with the definition of house but does change the definition of housing project, motion No. 1 seeks to amend Clause 1, line 20, which deals with the definition of housing project. By inserting the words "or homes" after the word "houses", motion No. 1 removes the dependence of CMHC on the definition of house as "building plus land". If houses must be on land, then the word "home" could be used to include dwellings that are not on land, such as floating homes.
Motion No. 1 would empower CMHC to insure mortgages for development projects of all types no matter where they are located, on land or water. It is hoped that in the future the National Housing Act could be amended to empower CMHC to insure mortgages on individual units rather than on whole communities. It is only a first step. There are many more things that need to be done to encourage the development of floating homes, but it would be a start toward overcoming the institutional bias against floating homes.
The purpose of motion No. 2 deals with the fact that there is nothing in the present wording of the interest deferment plan which prevents floating homes from being eligible for assistance. That is quite important. In the present wording, they are not left out. However, officials of CMHC have told my staff that residents of floating homes are not eligible. They have
made this policy decision 2,600 miles away from where the need is.
CMHC argues that the taxpayers should not subsidize luxury accommodation. Somehow, in their unfamiliarity with what house boats are on the west coast, they equate them with luxury accommodation. I do not believe that it is the mandate of CMHC to judge the quality of living accommodation on land or water. I do not believe that CMHC assesses the luxury of conventional houses before determining if they qualify for other programs. If the houses meet the criteria, the residents are deemed to qualify. To use the logic of CMHC, its officials should look at the quality of the broadloom and the furnishings in homes to judge whether the residents are living in luxurious surroundings before allowing them to qualify for government programs. I do not believe that CMHC should have this discretionary power.
CMHC also suggested that if the residents of floating homes are having financial difficulties, they should move on to land. CMHC officials of all people should know about the crisis in affordable housing in Vancouver before making such a suggestion. Their regional director is certainly well aware of the problem.
1 also think it is unacceptable for CMHC to be telling Canadians where and how they should be living, provided that their home complies with municipal regulations and standards. This is clearly one of the problems with centrally-administered national programs. National institutions must be sensitive to regional needs. In the lower mainland area of British Columbia, regional needs include floating homes and a marine coast.
For all these reasons, I urge members of the House to support these amendments and extend equal treatment to home owners inventive enough to use the only space available to them in many areas, that is, marine space.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an important and a proud day, proud not only for the government but for all members of the House who have been associated with supporting Bill C-89. Most of all, it is a day that will show some ray of hope for thousands of Canadian families and individuals seeking assistance with housing and employment needs.
As I indicated in my remarks the day after the budget was introduced, November 13, Bill C-89 is a sensible and sensitive response to the needs that I have described. For many Canadians this is a very important piece of legislation. I predict, as 1 have throughout the many days and evenings of discussion with my colleagues in the House, that this bill will have a significant impact, not only on housing problems and conditions of Canadians, but on the economy and the provision of employment in that sector.
In short, Bill C-89 does four major things. First, it enables the Canada mortgage renewal plan to proceed without delay. Second, it allows the Canada rental supply plan to move toward operation. Third, it contains provisions which will be of
March 31, 1982

interest to all home owners, but especially to first-time home buyers. 1 will expand on that shortly. Fourth, it will enable Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to conduct its activities in a more efficient and, indeed, a more compassionate manner.
It provides very important steps needed to enable the government to deal effectively with housing issues, and as such it is very important to all participants in the housing market such as home owners, prospective home owners, rental entrepreneurs, renters, those seeking rental accommodation upon family formation, the building industry and the lending institutions which serve the industry.
Of equal concern is the situation of those who are concerned about rental accommodations, both its provision and its supply as well as its affordability. There is concern among lower income families about the availability of rental units and the amount they will have to pay for them. This government will be assisting in the construction of approximately 55,000 rental units in Canada this year which are comprised of 25,000 units under the non-profit and co-operative housing program under section 56(1) which supports co-operative and non-profit construction, as well as 30,000 units which have been identified under the Canada rental supply plan. These units have been identified by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and provided for by him through the commitment of $350 million in the next two fiscal periods.
1 would remind hon. members that of the 30,000 units to be supported by the Canada rental supply plan one third are designated to serve Canadians on a rent-geared-to-income basis. It is obvious in the case of those provinces which will cooperate and assist in that rent-geared-to-income program, which is specifically designed to assist Canadians who are seeking affordable accommodations, that there could hardly be a more equitable program than the rent-geared-to-income program which is in place and being further supported by the Canada rental supply plan.
I do not believe that I have to dwell any longer on the economic impact of the Canada rental supply plan in the housing market and the opportunities which it will provide to those working in the housing industry. I am sure that those members who have longer experience in the House and in this business understand well the immediate impact that the construction of 30,000 multiple units will have on Canadians from coast to coast.
There are two other features of the bill which I would like to address. First, I will discuss the topic of mortgage instruments and the provisions in the bill which would enable Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to facilitate the development of new mortgage instruments. As we arc all aware, the term of the mortgage instrument had declined from 25 years to 5 years, and now to one year-in some cases for even a shorter period of time. This has increased uncertainty for mortgage borrowers and has almost totally reduced the security which home owners used to have with fixed monthly payments over that period of time. This has made it much more difficult for
Housing
rental entrepreneurs who need five-year mortgage money because rental production is not economically viable to them for construction in the short run. The reason for this is that investors in mortgages do not want to invest in longer term investments only to see the investment returns increase in the future. This situation of volatile mortgage interest rates has resulted in considerable attention to new mortgage instruments such as the variable rate mortgage, shared equity or appreciation mortgage and price level adjusted mortgages.
I am pleased that this bill will enable CMHC to facilitate these new developments. These instruments do have the potential to improve the situation for both borrowers and investors; help to ensure the availability of longer term funds for mortgages and provide greater certainty of mortgage payments.
Another area dealt with by this legislation is the premiums which Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation can charge for mortgage insurance, which are presently set out in the act and cannot be changed except for an amendment to the act. This is one of the reasons why these changes to the National Housing Act must be made to introduce this additional flexibility so that CMHC can operate in the marketplace in a more business-like fashion.
Not only is it essential to the efficiency of the corporation, but, in turn, it gives a better return for the expense side of the operation of the corporation and thus a better return to the taxpayer who is supporting the government operation.
The bill now before us would allow CMHC to accept an assignment of mortgage in a default situation rather than obtaining possession. This is another provision of the bill which makes the corporation more efficient and thereby reduces the cost of operation to the government and the taxpayer. For example, in the case of a multiple unit housing project which is in temporary difficulty but which CMHC believes is a viable business proposition, the amendments would enable the corporation to move in a way which will ensure not only a tax saving to the taxpayer but will prevent inconvenience to tenants in such buildings. It would also permit another option. The amendments would also allow another claim settlement arrangement whereby lenders would be permitted to sell a property where, after close examination, it is deemed by the corporation, in consultation with the project owner, to be practical and feasible. As far as the mortgage insurance fund is concerned, the result would be that it would acquire fewer properties and the case load on the fund would be substantially reduced. Again, it would thereby reduce the cost to the corporation and the government which, as you know, has had to move to assess the corporation in the last few years because of the high demand of failures and hence claims on the fund.
The Canada mortgage renewal plan will and is presently being prepared for implementation by CMHC in anticipation of the passage of Bill C-89 before the House. I can assure the House that no time will be lost in taking advantage of the legislation, which hopefully the House will deal with today. A comprehensive public information program will be undertaken

March 31, 1982
Housing
so that individuals will be able to have access to programs as they pertain to their particular circumstance.
1 was interested to hear the explanation and the urging for the adoption of the amendments proposed this afternoon which were addressed by the first speaker. I would have to indicate that although the corporation has responded by initially indicating its concerns for the proposed amendments, I have not had an opportunity to receive advice from the corporation, nor have we had time seriously to consider the implications of the proposed amendments. Certainly the amendments proposed by the hon. member urge a sympathetic hearing but, as you can well recall, the member also indicated the difficulties which exist in accepting such amendments. Because the amendments were introduced at a late stage we cannot support them today.
I want to make one further comment about the remarks of the hon. member who addressed what was apparently an observation by officials of the corporation about the quality of housing. He said that the corporation or the government should really have no role and nothing to say about the quality of housing. An integral and very important part of the Canada rental supply plan is that it is designed so that the Canadian government and Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation can ensure that the 30,000 units constructed under that program with the $7,500 second mortgage are of modest construction. One of our major concerns is to ensure that the incentives under this plan will guarantee that modest accommodation is provided-not luxury accommodation but that which will provide affordable and modest rental homes. One of the features of the plan is that the corporation can exercise control to ensure that the quality of building is modest and at the same time attractive.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, I would urge all those Canadians who feel that the program may be of benefit to them, to investigate the options provided under it.
1 should like to thank my colleagues who have supported the legislation, Mr. Speaker. I should also like to thank members of the provincial legislatures who have indicated support for it and those various municipal officials who, in response to my communications offered support for it. I should like to thank the trade union organizations who indicated support for it and finally, the industry organizations such as CIPREC, UDI, and HUDAC, the traditional representative in the industry who, as we know, urged passage of the legislation as soon as possible.
The reward for adoption of this important legislation will be for me, as I am sure it will be for all members, the help it will offer to many thousands of Canadians seeking assistance in housing and in jobs.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to address the House briefly at third reading stage of this bill. The House will remember that this legislation is the result of a year and a half or two years of promises by the Liberal Party to do something to help Canadian home owners. From that standpoint we welcome the fact that it finally came about.
Throughout the summer and fall of 1980 and into 1981, Canadians saw mortgage interest rates that they had never seen before. They saw an increase in foreclosures and power of sale proceedings became a way of life for thousands and thousands of Canadians who previously had no idea of the force and effect of this remedy. Interest rates continue to cripple the housing industry. Many Canadians have seen their mortgage payments double as a result of the Liberal high interest rate policy. Thousands are abandoning their homes because they can no longer make the mortgage payments.
After marches on Parliament by Canadian home owners in the fall of 1981 we finally got a budget which, in most ways, was a disaster. If there was any glimmer of hope for Canadians, it was in the provisions of the bill that was passed before the House.
Interest rates still concern us, Mr. Speaker. Since the bill was introduced, CMHC brought forward its annual report dated March 12, 1982, which focused upon high interest rates in 1981 and what they have done to the Canadian housing market and the ability of Canadians to make mortgage payments. The corporation stated that it is very very difficult for first time home owners to participate in the current market. In 1981 there was a crisis in housing starts. The current prediction is for 152,000 starts this year, although for various reasons CMHC has suggested that we need 220,000 starts per year. There has been some suggestion that the number will be reduced to 200,000. Even at that rate we would still have 25 per cent or 30 per cent below what CMHC says we need to house Canadians properly.
I should like to draw the attention of the House to some things that are being done in other countries. In March 1982 the mortgage rate in Great Britain was 15 per cent. Housing societies there, which are like our trust companies, cut the interest rate on mortgages to 13.5 per cent. It is a shame that all we can get out of this government is that, through this bill, it will give an interest free deferral of up to $3,000 to home owners who have five per cent equity in their home, and to home owners who have no substantial equity in their home it will give a grant of up to $3,000. In order to qualify, home owners must pay more than 30 per cent of their income for principal, interest and property taxes. I remind the House that
Housing
this plan only applies to mortgages which mature between September 1, 1981 and November 11, 1982. If the government continues with its Liberal high interest rate policy, there is no question the minister will be back in the House next fall asking for an amendment to the act in order to redress the problems the government will have created for Canadians in the intervening eight or nine months.
The comparison of this legislation is interesting. We on this side suggested to Canadians that they had every right to treat mortgage interest and property tax as legitimate deductions from income, as was done in the United States and in Great Britain. We suggested that it was a legitimate deduction from income which Canadian home owners could use. The net result of the much maligned-and I say much maligned by the Liberal Party-Progressive Conservative mortgage interest and realty tax credit plan would have been, in 1982, to give Canadians with normal $35,000 mortgages a tax break, credit or payment of approximately $150 per month. If we examine the increases in the mortgage payments of ordinary Canadians as a result of the Liberal high interest rate policy, we find that our suggestion, which was before the House in the form of legislation, would have gone a long way toward overcoming the grief with which Canadians are faced today.
Now I turn to the area of vacancy rates. The vacancy rates created by the government have reached all-time crisis proportions. If one lives in Oshawa, one is faced with a vacancy rate of 0.0 per cent. If one lives in Hamilton, it is 0.7 per cent. The standard figure of 3.0 per cent is considered to be acceptable in order for Canadians, with the normal flow of people in and out of apartments, to find decent, affordable accommodation in which to live and raise their families. The bill suggests that interest-free loans of up to $7,500 per unit will be given to assist in the construction of 15,000 rental units. This was proposed in November, and in the intervening months between November and early March the government found, as it has with many of its predictions, that its prediction was not correct. Perhaps the government was fooled by the many holes in the ground, or the in again out again, now you see it now you don't attitude, created by MURBs. The holes and footings in the ground were considered to be housing starts, but suddenly the government realized that nothing would be erected over these holes, so it came forward with the promise of another
15,000	units in March. This promise was made in an announcement by the minister contained in a comprehensive release from his office, in which he talked about what the government would do for repairs of Canadian houses.
This is all very nice, but I think it is well understood that apartments or rental accommodations are not being built because of the Liberal high interest rate policy. There is no way that one can economically build rental units under the present high interest rates which the cabinet and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) are supporting as a tonic for Canadians. It is not much of a tonic, because we are not

receiving housing starts. Any Canadian involved in the development business realizes that apartments cannot be built with interest rates at the level at which the government is keeping them.
Unfortunately I did not have an opportunity to participate in all committee meetings which were held, but 1 have reviewed the remarks that were made. I should like to bring to the attention of the House that there is some hope for Canadians. The Minister of Finance firmly suggested in the budget that it was the intention of the Liberal government to tax Canadians on the imputed rental value of their homes. This was based upon budget figures which were brought forward by the minister. He said that it was not correct, according to the Liberal Party, that Canadians should own homes, should pay them off, and then should be able to get away with not paying income tax on the imputed value. The Minister of Finance stuck to his guns on this. He absolutely refused to say that at no time will the Liberal government tax Canadians on the imputed value of their homes. This now appears to us to be government policy as enunciated by the Minister of Finance. Quite frankly we are shocked.
We feel there is no reason that Canadians should be forced to pay income tax on income which they have not received in cash. We feel this Liberal concept of imputed rental value ignores significant costs associated with home ownership, such as maintenance, mortgage payments and realty taxes. This concept could force Canadians to lose their homes. We have seen far too many homes lost under Liberal government policies, and we on this side of the House do not want to see Canadians losing their homes. The Liberals who are forcing this socialist concept upon Canadians will find that the Progressive Conservative Party, in all probability, will fight hard to ensure that the imputed rent concept gets no further than any of the other proposals upon which the Minister of Finance has backtracked.

I have looked at this legislation in some detail. I am convinced it opens the way to even far greater problems than we already have. As a result of this legislation and other legislation which has at least been alluded to in recent days, we will undoubtedly see more and more Canadians assuming mortgage payments that will stretch their ability to pay to the limit. This stretching of their ability will result without question in their deferring principal and interest payments to another time when they hope they will earn more. When they make that deferral it will result in those people owing more at the end of any given year than they did at the beginning.
As a result of this legislation and this government's actions, and as a result of the interest rate policy Mr. Bouey is pursuing, we will see a repeat of the things which happened in the AHOP program. People were encouraged to buy homes they could not afford and assume responsibilities they could not handle. They put off the real cost of the home to a day five years down the road, and when that day arrived they found in so many cases that they were not earning enough to keep the home and they lost all of their investment.

They were encouraged to go in there by the government, and when they did so it was in the hope and expectation that their wages would continue to rise and they could cover the mortgage payments. speakeroldname: Mr. Henri Tousignant (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to take part in the debate on third reading of Bill C-89. Just like the United States and the European countries, Canada is going through difficult economic times. Our government is committed to make the fight against inflation and the recovery of Canadian economy the top priority until this aim is achieved. This determination of the government to counter inflationary pressures does not mean, however, that we do not recognize the importance of helping those who need it most.
Regarding housing, the budget of November 12 stated that the government would offer interest-free loans to assist in the construction of 15,000 rental units in those areas where the vacancy rate is very low. Last March 23, the hon. minister responsible for housing and public works announced that the government would allocate an additional amount of $100 million to increase from 15,000 to 30,000 the number of new units eligible for interest-free loans of up to $7,500 per unit. This will give more Canadians access to proper housing at affordable prices.
Moreover, the government has earmarked $30 million in interest-free loans for the improvement of existing houses. These funds will be allocated to the areas with the highest unemployment rates. Quebec alone will receive 43 per cent of the total budget, or $9.6 million. The new assistance program for housing renovations will supplement the $169 million already allocated for this purpose under the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, better known as RRAP, and differs from the latter in that the assistance will be directed to high unemployment areas. It will promote job creation because loan recipients will have to invest $7 for every
$3 of assistance granted. The renovation program will provide an incentive to the Canadian construction industry.
The government is also concerned with home owners who have to renew their mortgages and may lose their home because of higher interest rates. In that respect, the government has developed a plan under which if an individual has more than 5 per cent equity in his home and after having renewed his mortgage, considers that his mortgage payments plus property taxes exceed 30 per cent of family income before taxes, the approved lender could defer interest payments for a year, up to a maximum of $3,000. Where an individual has less than 5 per cent equity in his home, but his payments still exceed 30 per cent, that individual will also be entitled to a grant of up to the $3,000 maximum.
That plan applies to mortgage loans with maturity dates falling between September 1st, 1981 and November 1 1, 1982. These recent commitments as well as the existing programs will bring to 100,000 the estimated number of jobs that will be created directly or indirectly by the Canadian government's initiatives in the housing area.
Such initiatives are a tangible expression of this government's commitment to do all it can to remedy the precarious situation that prevails in rental housing, to help Canadians facing serious difficulties when renewing their mortgages, and to restore healthy economic growth.
Mr. Speaker, I listened earlier to opposition members who had reservations about this legislation, and I was tempted to laugh at all the proposals, suggestions and solutions which they were putting forward. The previous speaker, the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), referred to matters that can really affect all Canadians. His comments verged on demagogy, Mr. Speaker, for what could be more natural, Mr. Speaker, for Canadians than owning their own homes?
That is a fact!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:

They also raise the matter of the right to home ownership. Is there a more basic right than the right to home ownership? Tell me, are they not touching these people who speak from both sides of their mouths, Mr. Speaker? Why don't they say that it is all right to want to become a home owner, while it is not to want to buy a $75,000 home with only a $500 down payment? They would have to explain that. I feel it would be much more normal and make a lot more sense to tell people to buy instead less expensive homes, worth maybe between $45,000 and $50,000, and to make down payments somewhere between $15,000 and $20,000. But these people run around asking whether there is a more basic right than the right to home ownership and leaving all their listeners unsatisfied. There are others who refer to high interest rates, who blame the government for spending too much and who, in the same
March 31, 1982

breath, complain that the government is not spending enough on housing, saying that they support the bill, but that they would like to see the government spend more. Clearly, it is possible to deal with all the problems and cases piecemeal, one by one. Then, they come back after a while and complain that the deficit is too high and that the government should do something about it. Well, what do they really want?
Of course, just about any problem could be solved with a great deal of money, say $200, $400 or $500 million, whether in housing, agriculture, forestry or in the automobile industry. We are aware on this side of the House that problems exist and we can identify them. We have no masochistic reason to try to keep people in poverty and have them raise a hue and cry. We can identify all the problems which exist in Canada, but in order to solve them all overnight it takes money, and the people opposite are the first to tell us that the deficit is too high, that we spend too much. Then, Mr. Speaker, those people ought to become a bit more serious. Of course, I know they are not there to campaign for the government now in power, that is most obvious; but still, there comes a time when they should be a bit more honest in what they say, in what they do. So, I am being asked to speak on the price of gas. Of course, I am proud, and I thank the hon. member for throwing me a line. There again, that is what we hear from one end of the country to the other: "You, Liberals, you get elected by saying that the price of gas will not go up; now, look at how high it has gone. You beat us on the 18 cents".
Sky high!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Sky high! 1 say this to the hon. member. He knows full well that with a Progressive Conservatives government the price of gas would naturally have also gone up to 85 per cent of the world price. We, instead, said 75 per cent of the world price. Those are the facts. In addition, they were talking about an additional 18-cent tax. That is the truth of the matter.
So, naturally, just as the Progressive Conservatives and the Liberals had foreseen, the price of gas increased, just like the price of other consumer goods, such as bread, butter, etc. But they had planned an additional 18 cents. speechtext: Therefore, this will benefit a great number of Canadians who will have access to cheaper rental accommodation. Evidently, they cannot obtain them free of charge. Of course, this cannot be done. We cannot pay for everything and the minister cannot build those housing projects himself. This legislation will enable many Canadians to get cheaper and better rental units. It will also put some Canadians to work in the construction industry. It will give a new impetus to construction. In the present situation, the minister responsible for housing has almost worked a miracle, it is an amazing feat. I am quite pleased this has happened today and I hope that in a few minutes the bill will be given third reading.

This is the second opportunity I have had, Mr. Speaker, to rise to speak to this bill, C-89, to amend the National Housing Act and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act. I think back over the last year and the many times that members on this side have risen and put questions to the minister of housing. When is he going to help the home owner? When is he going to help the renter? The only answer we ever got from the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) was to wait until the budget comes.
The budget came on November 12 and we questioned him again and he said: "I am going to bring forth legislation." That legislation came forward on January 28. On March 2 when the bells commenced ringing and all of us on this side implored the government to continue the committee meetings, the government House leader would not allow it and the Minister of Public works would not allow his committee to meet either. We asked for that committee to meet in spite of the division bells ringing. Mr. Speaker, there are many people who have spoken out against the lack of action by the government.
The Toronto Home Builders' Association said the federal budget discontinued various incentives to private investment in Canada. We believe the Department of Finance was inadequately informed as to the negative impact that many changes would have on the housing market.
The Canadian Institute of Public Real Estate Companies said that high interest rates have made construction of new apartment buildings an unenviable proposition; in Ontario, to break even on a new building financed at today's figures a landlord would have to charge in the order of $800 a month for a typical one-bedroom apartment.
This bill does not address those problems. The CMHC estimates that between 210,000 and 220,000 housing starts are needed each year, yet the estimates of the number of starts is down around 160,000 to 170,000. I might indicate what the
